name: John Bunyan
title: John Bunyan: prison, conscience and The Pilgrim’s Progress
description: John Bunyan’s imprisonment and the publication of The Pilgrim’s Progress in 1678, with a specialist chronology and sources from Bedford.

sections.heading: A conscience that would not agree to stop preaching
paragraphs: John Bunyan was born in 1628 near Bedford and learned the trade of mending metal utensils. His religious journey led him to an independent congregation. With the restoration of the English monarchy in 1660, religious uniformity became a political issue once again, and preaching outside the established framework could lead to prison.

Bunyan was arrested in 1660. His refusal to promise to stop preaching prolonged his imprisonment until 1672. The museum’s history recalls that his wife Elizabeth tried to obtain a new hearing of the case. His family and his congregation also bore the consequences of that decision.

sections.heading: What prison could not shut in
paragraphs: During his years in prison, Bunyan wrote religious works, among them Grace Abounding, published in 1666. The museum preserves the memory of his work to help support the family and of the contacts he kept with the community. The image of a completely isolated writer does not, by itself, describe that experience.

The first part of The Pilgrim’s Progress appeared in 1678. The chronology by W. R. Owens and Anne Page distinguishes the stages of writing and publication. It is prudent to say that the book took shape during the years of hardship, without claiming that every page was written in the same cell or during a single period of imprisonment.

reflection: Hebrews 12:1–3 invites us to run with perseverance and to fix our eyes on Jesus. That exhortation offers a framework for reading the image of the pilgrim who walks on among obstacles. Bunyan’s story can keep the reader company because it acknowledges weariness and danger, as well as the longing to reach the destination.

The story of his imprisonment raises a question about conscience and religious freedom. Being faithful to a conviction can have consequences for those around us; acknowledging them takes humility. In remembering Bunyan, it is fitting to make room also for his family and his church, whose everyday help made part of his work possible.
review_note: The dates of certain stages of writing are approximate. The book is not copied, and its complete composition is not attributed to a single imprisonment.
source_labels: Bunyan Meeting and John Bunyan Museum, Bedford. “John Bunyan — Detailed History.”
